 Mini PCs offer a way to reclaim desk space without giving up the flexibility of a proper desktop. Whether you need an affordable machine for everyday work, a quiet computer for a shared room, a portable powerhouse or a compact gaming setup, there’s now a model to suit.
 Our mini PC expert, Anthony Spadafora, has been using many of the best mini PCs as an alternative to a laptop or a big, bulky desktop for the past seven years, and he's never looked back. The Mac mini M6 is now our top recommendation as the best mini PC, with incredible performance from Apple's chipset in its compact, sleek design. But if you're a fan of Windows, you'll be happy to know there are plenty of fantastic options to choose from today, like the recent Lenovo Yoga Mini .
 Whether you want a mini PC you can slip in your pocket or bag to travel with, something closer to a game console or as much power as possible in a tiny package, there’s something here for every budget and use case. We’ve tested the latest options across real-world use and benchmark workloads to find the mini PCs worth buying today.
 Soon, we'll see Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X chips enter the scene, considering these AI-focused processors are aimed at "small desktops." We've tested many RTX Spark laptops and are impressed with the results for local AI tasks, and we'll be going hands-on to see what these RTX Spark compact PCs have to offer, too.
 Why you can trust Tom's Guide 
 There's a lot to test when it comes to testing a mini PC, but here at Tom's Guide we know what we should be looking for. Why? Because we've been at it for 20 year's and our computing team has decades of combined experience. We've got Security and Home Ofiice Editor Anthony Spadafora , who swapped to a mini PC years ago and has never gone back since. Then there's Tony Polanco , Senior Computing Writer, who's been putting PCs to the test through a long and illustrious career at the likes of laptop mag, PC mag, and more.
 Here are the tests we put mini PCs through before they can make this list and get a recommendation.
 We use them as our primary machine. These are computers that you're going to be using for everything, so we want to make sure they're good at it. We swap out our main machines and use them for our heavy workloads. If they can do that, they'll be good for most people.
 We lab test them. We send them to the Tom's Guide testing labs, where they're put through a bunch of stress testing and benchmarks to see just how well they perform.
 We compare them to the competition. There's no point putting them on the list unless they offer a better experience than what we recommend here. So we put them side by side, use them and compare their specs. Is it better? There's a new entry for the list.

All that in a compact form factor and with the freedom of choosing your go-to mouse, keyboard and monitor? The mini PC revolution has arrived, and we've done all the testing to pick the finest ones around.

 It's been a long time coming, but Apple's Mac mini got a major upgrade, and its standout performance shows it was certainly worth the wait. The Mac mini M6 features Apple's next-gen silicon in a familiar yet hugely welcome sleek and compact design, and it now surpasses the already great Mac mini M4 to become the best mini PC we recommend.
 The Mac mini got a significant performance boost thanks to the 2-nanometer (nm) M6 chip, which translated to a whopping 44% jump over the previous M4 chip in our testing. In fact, despite the M6 being the base chip, it nearly catches up to the pro-level M4 Pro processor, which says a lot considering the price difference between the two. In our tester Anthony's typical daily workload, which involves having dozens of Chrome tabs open along with photo editing, the Mac mini M6 didn't break a sweat.
 Even better? This mini PC is also a hugely capable gaming machine, considering it can play the likes of Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p with 56 fps. Of course, it's better suited for 1080p gaming, but you can get a lot out of gaming on the Mac mini despite it not having a dedicated graphics card.

 The Geekom A5 2025 Edition is our top pick for the best budget mini PC, thanks to its surprisingly affordable price and just how much performance you get for $300. While our previous pick is impressive, the Kamrui E3B , this mini PC is $100 cheaper and just as capable for browsing the web, office work and even some light gaming. Just like with the E3B, Anothny used this refreshed version of the Geekom A5 as his daily driver for a month with a dual-monitor setup, and despite his more demanding workload, it held its own even with a less powerful AMD Ryzen 5 chip, Radeon Vega 7 integrated graphics and 16GB of DDR4 memory.
 In addition to its excellent price-to-performance, Geekom decided to do something different with the A5 by giving it a rose gold colorway instead of the typical silver and black you see on most other mini PCs. It also has a pattern of lined cutouts on either side for extra ventilation, along with a reflective chrome edge up top, which gives it a more premium look overall. While Geekom does include a VESA mounting bracket so that you can tuck the A5 behind a monitor, its sleek and colorful design makes it much better suited for a well-earned place on your desk.

 At 4.61 x 4.41 x 1.94 inches, the Geekom A5 is slightly larger than the A6 but still smaller than Apple’s Mac mini M6 . Despite its small footprint, this mini PC comes packed with ports at the front and back, but there’s also an SD card reader on the right side and a Kensington lock on the left side. Up front, you get two USB-A ports and a headphone jack, but it’s around back where things really get impressive, especially for a budget mini PC. The A5 has two more USB-A ports there, along with dual HDMI 2.0 ports, two USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 ports, and something you rarely see at this price: a 2.5 gigabit Ethernet port.
 Add it all up, and this little mini PC can power a quad-monitor setup. While it comes with a 512GB SSD and 16GB of memory, it’s really easy to open up the case and upgrade its existing components, but you can also add another M.2 SSD as well as a 2.5-inch HDD or SSD.
 If you’re looking to downsize from a bulky desktop or ditch an older laptop, the Geekom A5 is an excellent choice, especially at this price, granted your workflow isn’t too demanding. However, if it is, we'd suggest saving up a bit more for the A6, which is significantly faster but also a bit smaller, too. For those who want to dive into the world of mini PCs without overpaying or just want a capable device with a pop of color, the A5 is easy to recommend.

 The Geekom A9 Max 2025 Edition was already a powerhouse, but the latest model steps it all up a notch — all while staying impressively cool and quiet under pressure.

Four USB-A ports line the front for easy access, with a further two USB-A, two HDMI 2.1, and dual USB4 ports on the rear, making it one of the most connectivity-rich options available.
 Under the hood, Geekom loads the A9 Max with 32GB of DDR5 RAM and its upgraded IceBlast 3.0 cooling — a combo that kept performance reliably high in our extended testing. Using it as his daily workstation, Anthony found it impressively responsive even under heavy multitasking, with the Radeon 890M integrated graphics delivering a very playable experience in titles like Death Stranding 2 at 1080p. Better yet, the new cooling system meant the internal fan stayed whisper-quiet, even as the system powered through real-world workloads.

 Anthony Spadafora prefers desktops to laptops, and when you're short on space, a mini PC is the perfect solution. After building his own small form factor PCs for years, he started testing and reviewing pre-built mini PCs as part of his work at Tom's Guide. Anthony also covers standing desks, office chairs and other home office furniture, and his work with mini PCs ensures he's able to put together brand-new desk setups to show off all the tiny computers that he goes hands-on with.
 Best Mini PCs: Frequently Asked Questions 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Can a mini PC replace a desktop computer?
 Yes, a mini PC can replace a traditional desktop for web browsing, office work, streaming, video calls and many creative or multitasking workloads, provided you choose hardware that suits the job. 
 For serious PC gaming, GPU-intensive creation or workloads needing lots of expansion, a conventional desktop will still offer better performance and upgrade headroom. That said, mini PCs are only getting more powerful. Be sure to check the processor, graphics, memory, storage, ports and monitor support when choosing.
 Should I buy a Mac mini or a Windows mini PC?
 Buy a Mac mini if you want macOS, use Apple services or software, and value the Mac mini M6’s very strong all-round performance and compact design. 
 Buy a Windows mini PC if you need Windows-only software, want broader game support or prioritise hardware choice, ports and user-upgradeable memory or storage. 
 While we recommend the Mac mini M6 as the mini PC for most, Windows alternatives cover plenty of different needs, for lower-cost, gaming, quiet-operation and workstation-focused needs. 
 Are mini PCs good for gaming?
 Yes, some mini PCs are good for gaming, but the right choice depends on the games, resolution and settings you expect to use. Integrated graphics can suit lighter or less demanding games, while modern AAA games benefit from a model with a capable discrete GPU. That's why we recommend the Minisforum G1 Pro for gaming, because of its desktop-grade Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 GPU.
 You'll find that the G1 Pro reached 45.2 fps in Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p in our tests, and even the Mac mini M6 can reach up to 56.9 fps! That said, you won't find a big selection of games if you opt for a Mac over Windows. 
 Do mini PCs come with a monitor, keyboard and mouse?
 Usually, a mini PC is sold as the computer only, so you will normally need to provide a monitor, keyboard and mouse separately. You may also need to check whether the listed configuration includes storage, memory or an operating-system licence, particularly with more configurable models like the Framework Desktop . 
 Factor those extras into the total cost and confirm that the PC has the ports or wireless connectivity your display and accessories require. Wondering what's worth getting? Check out our guides on the best monitor , best keyboard and best mouse . 
 How much RAM do I need in a mini PC?
 For everyday browsing, office work and streaming, 16GB of RAM is a sensible target; demanding multitasking, creative work, local AI tasks or heavier gaming may justify 32GB or more. 
 RAM cannot always be upgraded later, so consider your likely needs over the life of the PC. Of course, adding extra RAM is getting expensive due to RAMaggedon , so know what you're going to use a PC for to make sure you're not overspending on performance you don't need. 
 Is it worth buying an AI PC?
 An AI PC is worth buying if you intend to use local AI models and agents for complex coding, creative work, repetitive workflows and more with absolute data privacy. For everyday tasks such as researching on the web, writing up documents, replying to emails and gaming, you won't need an AI PC. 
 Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X chip is coming to small desktops, and while this chip comes with amazing performance for offline AI work, along with 3D creative work and gaming on a single processor, it's aimed at pro-level users who can take full advantage of its local AI workloads. We asked a tech expert who RTX Spark laptops are for , with Tom Mainelli, Group Vice President of Device & Consumer Research at IDC, stating, "These are outside the budget and needs of mainstream users, for now."
 Many of the mini PCs we recommend are capable of AI work, including the Mac mini M6 and Geekom A9 Max 2026 , but they go beyond just local AI tasks. For general workflows, an AI PC isn't needed. 
 How to choose the best mini PC for you 
 Mini PCs range from small project PCs for under $50 to compact desktops that can cost anywhere between $500 to $1,500 or even more.
 Stick PCs are the most versatile, and generally cost between $100 (£100/AU$150) and $200 (£200/$AU300), and will work with most TVs or monitors, though we don't normally recommend them.
 Mini PC prices vary considerably based on their hardware and come in all sorts of different form factors, but for the most part, the small, rectangular-shaped ones are the most popular, and you won't have a hard time finding one to fit your own particular needs.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Know what you want 
 Finding the right mini PC for you starts with knowing what you're looking for. Do you want something small enough to tuck behind a TV as a dedicated streaming box, or are you looking for something with gaming capabilities? Do you want a basic internet-browsing machine, or do you need serious processing and graphics capabilities?
 Our best picks above do a good job of highlighting the use cases different systems are best suited to, and that should help you narrow down your choices.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Find the right size 
 Then there's the question of form factor. Mini PCs are all small, but there is a range of options within the category, from PCs small enough to slip into your pocket to desktop towers that are still compact enough to stow out of sight.
 You'll sacrifice power for a smaller system, but you can still get a capable desktop that's small enough to carry in a backpack, even if you're after one well-suited for gaming or workstation performance.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Make sure you like your configuration and upgrade options 
 Finally, you want to look at configuration options and upgradability.
 Many mini PCs have two or three configuration options, which can change everything from the amount of included storage to the presence of high-end processors and discrete graphics cards.
 There's also the question of upgrades. Many of the smallest mini PCs leave no room for future hardware changes, but others are designed to let you add memory or storage, or even come outfitted with ports that allow you to attach an external GPU for better graphics and gaming performance.
 When in doubt, check our reviews, which include configuration details and will discuss the potential for future upgrades.
 ▲ Back to the top 
 How we test the best mini PCs 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) We put every mini PC we review through a series of benchmark tests and weeks to months of real-world use to get the clearest picture we can of how well it performs, what use cases it's best suited to and what sort of capabilities you get for the price.
 For performance, we use the Geekbench processor test to measure a system's overall capabilities. We then test a device's file transfer speeds, copying large files to see how long it takes to copy multimedia files, documents and other content.
 To test graphics capabilities, we run several benchmark tests from 3DMark. If a system is properly equipped, we'll also run individual game tests to assess how well a particular mini PC handles the demands of modern gaming across a variety of resolutions and graphics settings.
 Most importantly, we spend a lot of time simply using each mini PC for everyday activities. We do work, browse the web, transfer files, play games and more, all to get a better sense of which ones are really worth your money.

 Questions to answer first
 1 How much data exists across every home PC, Mac, phone, and external drive? 
 2 How many years of file history and snapshots should remain available? 
 3 Where will the independent second copy live? 
 How to choose
 Start with current data, add three to five years of growth, then keep roughly 20% free.
 Choose two bays for a simple mirror; choose four bays when capacity will grow or multiple jobs share the NAS.
 Prefer straightforward backup software and administration over unused processor features.
 Avoid these mistakes
 Treating RAID as the only backup
 Buying raw capacity instead of protected capacity
 Ignoring restore testing
 Frequently asked questions
 Is a 2-bay NAS running RAID 1 a complete backup solution?
 No. A mirror keeps a copy on each disk so the NAS can usually continue after one disk fails. Deletion, malware, theft, and enclosure failure can affect both copies. Keep versioned backups on a separate USB disk, another NAS, or a cloud destination, with at least one copy off-site. Test that you can restore a file before relying on the setup.
 What is the best NAS for backing up multiple Mac (Time Machine) and Windows PCs?
 Our entry DS223 build fits ordinary file backup and Mac Time Machine when a 4TB mirror is enough. Choose the DS925+ when you need more capacity, spare bays, or supported business backup packages. Check each Windows backup application against the exact NAS model: Synology Drive file sync is different from a full computer image, and Active Backup for Business is not available on every DiskStation.
 How much usable storage do I actually get from 2×4TB or 4×12TB drives?
 Two 4TB disks in RAID 1 provide 4TB decimal capacity, equivalent to about 3.64TiB before system and filesystem overhead. Four 12TB disks in RAID 5 provide 36TB, about 32.74TiB before overhead. TB and TiB are different units; that conversion is not space lost to formatting. Leave room for backup versions, snapshots, and future growth.
 Synology vs. UGREEN for beginner home backup: Which is easier?
 Choose Synology when its integrated backup applications match your computers and you value a familiar administration workflow. UGREEN can offer more CPU and networking for the budget, but check application support and the recovery process before choosing on specifications alone. Both need updates, alerts, and restore tests; neither is maintenance-free.
 How do I protect my NAS backup against ransomware and sudden power outages?
 Use separate administrator and backup accounts, versioned backups, and an off-site or offline copy. Snapshots help recover older versions; immutable retention is a separate feature that must be supported by the exact model and configured correctly. A compatible UPS with tested automatic shutdown can reduce interruption risk. Neither snapshots nor a UPS guarantees recovery on its own.

A network-attached storage (NAS) box used to be a thing only IT hobbyists owned. In 2026 it is closer to a household appliance: a small always-on computer with hard drive bays that stores your files, streams your media, and runs the little services that keep a connected home humming. But "best home NAS" is a trick question, because the right pick depends entirely on what you plan to do with it.

This guide skips the spec-sheet overload and organizes the decision around how real people actually use a NAS at home. We will look at who genuinely needs one, walk through three common scenarios, and name a best pick for each.

Who Needs This?

You probably want a NAS if any of these sound like you. First, you are tired of juggling external USB drives and cloud subscriptions and want one private place for everything. Second, you take a lot of photos and video and have outgrown free cloud tiers. Third, you want to stream your own movie and music collection to TVs and phones around the house without monthly streaming fees. Fourth, you want automatic, redundant backups of multiple computers so a single drive failure never costs you data.

You probably do not need one if you own a single laptop, store little, and are happy paying for a cloud plan. For that life, a USB SSD plus cloud sync is simpler and cheaper. A NAS earns its keep when you have multiple devices, multiple people, or a growing media library. If that is you, browse current models on the Newegg NAS selection to see what fits your budget.

Use-Case Scenarios

Scenario 1: Simple backup and photo vault. You want a reliable, low-effort place to back up two or three computers and offload your phone's photo roll. You are not running heavy apps and you do not stream much. Here, two drive bays in a mirror (RAID 1) are plenty, low power draw matters, and ease of setup beats raw horsepower.

Scenario 2: Plex / Jellyfin media server. You have a movie, TV, and music library and want to stream it to TVs, tablets, and phones, sometimes to several screens at once. The deciding factor is the processor and whether it has hardware transcoding and an HDMI port, plus enough bays to hold a large library that keeps growing.

Scenario 3: Power-user home server. You want to run Docker containers, virtual machines, smart-home dashboards, a personal cloud, and maybe self-hosted apps, all at once. You need a strong CPU, generous and upgradable RAM, fast 2.5GbE or 10GbE networking, and NVMe slots for caching.

Best Pick per Scenario

Best for simple backup: Synology DS224+. This is the friendly entry point. It is a 2-bay unit built around a quad-core Intel Celeron at 2.0 GHz with 2GB of DDR4 (expandable to 6GB). Synology's DSM software is the easiest in the category, and its Active Backup and Photos apps handle exactly the "back up my computers and phone" job this scenario describes. Two bays in RAID 1 give you redundancy without overspending. It is available on Newegg, with MSRP around $370 (commonly sold lower).

Best for media server: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus. For Plex and Jellyfin, this 4-bay unit punches above its price. It runs an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 (a 5-core 12th-gen chip with quick-sync hardware transcoding), ships with 8GB of DDR5, and crucially pairs one 10GbE port with one 2.5GbE port plus a 4K-capable HDMI output. Four bays support up to roughly 144TB of raw capacity, with two NVMe slots for caching. Expect a price around $620, available on Newegg. If you prefer the most polished media app ecosystem instead, the QNAP TS-464 (quad-core Celeron N5095/N5105, 8GB DDR4, HDMI 2.1, dual 2.5GbE) is a strong alternative, available on Newegg.

Best for power-user home server: Synology DS925+ or TerraMaster F4-424 Pro. If you live in the Synology ecosystem and want rock-solid software for Docker, Virtual Machine Manager, and surveillance, the DS925+ is the pick: a 4-bay unit with a quad-core AMD Ryzen V1500B, 4GB ECC DDR4 expandable to 32GB, dual 2.5GbE, and two M.2 slots. MSRP is about $620, available on Newegg. If you want the most raw compute for the money and are comfortable with TerraMaster's TOS software, the F4-424 Pro is a beast for the class: an 8-core Intel Core i3-N305, 32GB of DDR5, four bays, and dual 2.5GbE, with a US price around $699, available on Newegg. The Synology wins on software polish; the TerraMaster wins on horsepower per dollar.

The Drives Matter Too

Whichever enclosure you choose, remember that most home NAS units ship diskless, so you buy the hard drives separately. For an always-on box, use drives rated for 24/7 NAS duty rather than standard desktop drives. You can compare capacities and warranties across the Newegg NAS hard drive selection and plan to fill at least two bays so you can run a mirror from day one.

Verdict

There is no single best home NAS for 2026, only the best one for your scenario. If you just want painless backups and a private photo library, the Synology DS224+ is the easy, affordable answer. If your home revolves around streaming your own media, the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus delivers transcoding muscle and fast networking at a fair price. And if you are the household tinkerer running containers and virtual machines, step up to the Synology DS925+ for software polish or the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro for sheer performance. Match the box to the job, add NAS-rated drives, and you will have a private cloud that pays for itself in a year or two.

Do I really need a NAS at home?
A NAS is worth it if you have multiple devices or people, a growing photo and video library, or want automatic redundant backups and private media streaming. If you own a single laptop and are happy with a cloud plan, a USB SSD plus cloud sync is simpler and cheaper.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is a 2-bay NAS running RAID 1 a complete backup solution?
 No. A mirror keeps a copy on each disk so the NAS can usually continue after one disk fails. Deletion, malware, theft, and enclosure failure can affect both copies. Keep versioned backups on a separate USB disk, another NAS, or a cloud destination, with at least one copy off-site. Test that you can restore a file before relying on the setup.
 What is the best NAS for backing up multiple Mac (Time Machine) and Windows PCs?
 Our entry DS223 build fits ordinary file backup and Mac Time Machine when a 4TB mirror is enough. Choose the DS925+ when you need more capacity, spare bays, or supported business backup packages. Check each Windows backup application against the exact NAS model: Synology Drive file sync is different from a full computer image, and Active Backup for Business is not available on every DiskStation.
 How much usable storage do I actually get from 2×4TB or 4×12TB drives?
 Two 4TB disks in RAID 1 provide 4TB decimal capacity, equivalent to about 3.64TiB before system and filesystem overhead. Four 12TB disks in RAID 5 provide 36TB, about 32.74TiB before overhead. TB and TiB are different units; that conversion is not space lost to formatting. Leave room for backup versions, snapshots, and future growth.
 Synology vs. UGREEN for beginner home backup: Which is easier?
 Choose Synology when its integrated backup applications match your computers and you value a familiar administration workflow. UGREEN can offer more CPU and networking for the budget, but check application support and the recovery process before choosing on specifications alone. Both need updates, alerts, and restore tests; neither is maintenance-free.
 How do I protect my NAS backup against ransomware and sudden power outages?
 Use separate administrator and backup accounts, versioned backups, and an off-site or offline copy. Snapshots help recover older versions; immutable retention is a separate feature that must be supported by the exact model and configured correctly. A compatible UPS with tested automatic shutdown can reduce interruption risk. Neither snapshots nor a UPS guarantees recovery on its own.

 Buffalo’s LinkStation 220D is a versatile and affordable NAS drive that’s suitable for both home and business users. But, as we’ve seen with Buffalo in the past, its products sometimes lack the straightforward ease of use that Mac and iOS users take for granted.
 The LinkStation 220D is a dual-bay NAS drive that houses two separate hard drives. You can buy it ‘unpopulated’ – with no drives at all – and then provide the drives that you want to use for yourself. Alternatively, you can buy it with 2TB, 4TB or 8TB.
 There’s also a more expensive model called the 220DR that’s designed for use with Western Digital’s high-speed Red drives, but the standard 220D model that we review here should be perfectly adequate for most homes and small businesses.
 The dual-bay setup also means you can use the LinkStation as a RAID drive, supporting either RAID 0 for maximum performance, or RAID 1 for maximum data protection (storing separate copies of your data on both drives). Future upgrades are simple as well, as you can quickly remove the front panel of the LinkStation and pull out the drives by their handles, with no screws or tools required. There’s also a USB port on the back of the LinkStation that can be used to make additional backups to an external USB drive for extra safety.
 Getting started is quite straightforward, as the 4TB LinkStation that we tested automatically showed up on our office network once we connected it to our router with an Ethernet cable. That allowed us to simply drag-and-drop files onto the LinkStation for quick backups, but things get a bit more complicated when you start to move beyond the basics. The LinkStation does work with Time Machine so that you can back up your Macs over the network, but setting up Time Machine and a ‘shared folder’ for your backups proved rather complicated.
 Buffalo’s NAS Navigator app for Macs allows you to view the LinkStation on your network and displays basic information, such as its IP address. However, using any other features requires you to open up a web browser in order to view the LinkStation’s web interface.
 This does include a variety of useful features, including Time Machine support, remote ‘web access’ for when you’re away from home or the office, BitTorrent downloads, and the ability to use the LinkStation as an iTunes server for streaming your music across the network. But this browser interface is very complicated and won’t be easy for non-technical users to understand – and Buffalo’s 125-page jargon-heavy PDF manual doesn’t really make life any easier.
 And neither do Buffalo’s mobile apps. Buffalo provides two separate apps for iOS devices: Smartphone Navigator for basic setup, and WebAccess to provide access to your files via Wi-Fi when you’re out and about.
 These apps are getting on a bit, and some users have complained that they’re unreliable. In fact, the apps seemed to run on our office iPhone and iPad without any problems, but they’re still quite complicated and unhelpful for people who aren’t familiar with NAS drives and networking technology.
 So while the LinkStation is a good option for more experienced home or business users who already know a bit about NAS drives, it’s probably not the best option for first-time users who are still learning the ropes.
 How to choose a NAS drive
 Here are some essential features you should look out for when selecting a NAS drive for your Mac.
 macOS compatibility and Time Machine support
 One of the great unsung features of macOS is Time Machine, the software that sits inside your System Preferences panel and quietly performs an automatic backup of the entire contents of your Mac’s hard disk every hour, on the hour.
 If you accidentally delete a file you can go back and check out all the previous versions of that file that you backed up in the past. And if your Mac starts behaving oddly and you think you might have been infected by malware, you can just reboot your Mac and use Time Machine to restore the entire macOS to an earlier, untarnished state.
 But, of course, in order to use Time Machine you do need to have an external hard drive connected to your Mac that can store all your old backups. Hard drives are pretty cheap these days, but as we all start to own more and more desktop computers, laptops and mobile devices, it starts to become both expensive and rather impractical to buy a separate backup drive for every single device in our home or office. The answer to this problem is a NAS drive.
 Most NAS drives are ‘Mac-compatible’ – but not all of them are what we might call ‘Mac-friendly’. For instance, not all NAS drives will allow you to use Time Machine to make backups over the network, so support for Time Machine is a key feature that you should check on when thinking about buying a NAS drive for use with one or more Macs.
 User accounts and sharing
 Another important feature is the ability to create individual user accounts, so that each person in your home or office can have their own private area on the NAS drive for storing their personal files. And, at the same time, it’s also handy to create ‘shares’, which are like public folders that can be shared by everyone – perhaps for storing music or photos for the whole family.
 Most NAS drives will allow you to do this, but sometimes you need a bit of network know-how to figure out how each drive handles this process (and some drives, such as Apple’s now-discontinued Time Capsule, just ignore this side of things altogether and focus on the basic task of handling Time Machine backups).
 Mobile device support
 And, of course, you’ll also want to check that your new NAS drive provides an app for your iPhone or iPad. Most of us now tend to use iCloud for backing up photos, videos and other files from our mobile devices, but it can give you extra peace of mind to know that you’ve got a spare backup on your NAS drive in case anything goes wrong.
 A good NAS drive will also let you share your photos and videos with other people by streaming them to mobile devices over your network, or possibly even provide a remote access option that allows you to retrieve files over the internet when you’re away from home (a feature that manufacturers often refer to as a ‘personal cloud’).
 File streaming
 Many people also use their NAS drive as a kind of central media server for their home, perhaps streaming music and videos to a games console that is connected to their TV in the front room. Mac users should check to see if a NAS drive can stream files to an Apple TV, or act as an ‘iTunes server’, storing your iTunes/Music library on the NAS drive so that it can stream music to every Mac or iOS device on the network.
 How much storage do you need?
 That’s something you’ll need to decide for yourself, but it’s worth mentioning that some NAS drives are more flexible on this point than others.
 Some of the less expensive NAS drives are sold with a built-in hard drive—generally at least 2TB—but the hard drive is fixed and can’t be replaced once it’s full (although the NAS drive may have a USB port that lets you connect a conventional USB hard drive in order to add some extra storage). This is the simplest option, favored by most home users and small businesses, as it means you can just unpack the NAS drive and connect it to your router to get started.
 Choosing the right number of drive bays
 When selecting a Network Attached Storage (NAS) device, two of the most critical decisions you’ll make are the number of drive bays and the RAID configuration. These choices directly impact your storage capacity, data redundancy, and overall performance. 
 The number of bays in a NAS enclosure determines how many hard drives (HDDs) or solid-state drives (SSDs) you can install. This choice depends on your current storage needs, plans for future expansion, and your desired RAID setup.
 Two-Bay NAS : A two-bay NAS is a common starting point for home users and small businesses. It allows for a basic RAID 1 configuration, which mirrors data across two drives for redundancy. This means if one drive fails, your data is safe on the other.
 Four-Bay NAS : A four-bay NAS is often recommended for those who need more storage, such as professionals, content creators, or small offices. With four bays, you can use more advanced RAID levels like RAID 5 or RAID 6, which offer a balance of storage efficiency and protection against one or two drive failures, respectively. Some four-bay models can support up to 80TB of storage and may offer expansion modules to add even more bays later.
 Larger NAS Units : For more demanding requirements, NAS devices with six, eight, or more bays are available, offering massive storage potential—up to 256TB in some cases.
 Many NAS devices are sold “unpopulated,” meaning you must purchase the drives separately. This provides the flexibility to choose your own drives and upgrade them in the future. 
 Selecting a RAID Configuration
 RAID (Redundant Array of Inexpensive Disks) is a technology that combines multiple drives into a single logical unit to improve performance or provide data redundancy . The RAID level you choose is often dictated by the number of drives you have and your priorities for speed versus data safety.
 Here are some common RAID configurations supported by NAS devices:
 RAID 0 (Striping) : This configuration combines two or more drives to maximize performance and capacity . Data is “striped” across the drives, leading to faster read and write speeds . However, RAID 0 offers no redundancy; if a single drive fails, all data in the array is lost . It is best suited for tasks where speed is paramount and data is backed up elsewhere .
 RAID 1 (Mirroring) : This setup requires at least two drives and creates an exact copy (or mirror) of your data on each drive . It provides excellent data protection, as you can simply replace a failed drive and rebuild the array . The trade-off is that your usable capacity is only half of the total raw capacity of the drives .
 RAID 5 : Requiring a minimum of three drives, RAID 5 stripes data across the drives along with parity information . This allows the array to withstand the failure of a single drive without any data loss . It offers a good balance of performance, storage efficiency (you lose the capacity of one drive for parity), and redundancy . Reads are typically fast, but writes can be slower due to the need to calculate and write parity data .
 RAID 6 : This level is similar to RAID 5 but requires at least four drives and uses dual parity . This means it can tolerate the failure of up to two drives simultaneously, offering even greater data protection .
 RAID 10 (or 1+0) : A hybrid RAID, this configuration combines the mirroring of RAID 1 with the striping of RAID 0 . It requires at least four drives and provides both high performance and redundancy, but at the cost of using only 50% of the total drive capacity .JBOD (Just a Bunch of Disks): This is not a true RAID level. It simply combines multiple drives into a single large volume without any performance or redundancy benefits
 Choosing between HDDs and SSDs
 While traditional HDDs are the most cost-effective solution for bulk storage in a NAS, SSDs are also an option .
 HDDs : Hard drives offer large capacities at a lower cost, making them ideal for storing large media libraries or backups. It’s important to use drives specifically designed for NAS use, as they are built for continuous operation and are more resistant to vibration. However, be aware that some recording technologies, like SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording), are unsuitable for RAID configurations and can cause errors.
 SSDs: Solid-state drives offer significantly faster performance and are quieter than HDDs. However, they are more expensive and typically have lower capacities, maxing out around 4TB for NAS-specific models . Some NAS devices allow you to use NVMe SSDs as a high-speed cache to boost the performance of an HDD array.
 The unpopulated option
 However, many NAS drives are sold ‘unpopulated’—without any internal hard drives already installed—and simply provide two or more empty drive bays into which you insert your own choice of hard drives. This option is more expensive, but it allows you to customise the NAS by buying your own hard in order to provide as much storage as you need. And, if you run out of storage space, you can just take out the old drives and insert new, larger drives in the future.
 This type of NAS drive generally also offers a number of ‘RAID’ options—this stands for “redundant array of independent disks”—which use multiple hard drives to provide additional performance and data protection.
 How we test NAS drives
 To evaluate Network-Attached Storage (NAS) drives, our testing process combines standardized benchmarking with practical, real-world use cases to ensure a comprehensive assessment.
 Our methodology involves several key steps:
 Benchmarking : We conduct stringent tests and benchmarks on the NAS drives we review. This allows us to build a library of results for direct comparison across different models .
 Real-World Simulation : We mirror everyday usage by transferring various sets of files and folders to and from the NAS device .
 Speed Tests : During these transfers, we specifically measure both write and read speeds to gauge performance.
 Large File Transfers : We also test how the drives perform during large file transfers, which is a common use case for NAS devices.
 In addition to performance, a crucial factor for Mac users is compatibility with macOS features. We specifically look for robust Time Machine support, as this allows for seamless, automatic backups of your entire Mac. While most NAS drives are “Mac-compatible,” not all are what we would consider “Mac-friendly” in their integration and ease of use.
 The setup process is also a consideration. Unlike simple plug-and-play external drives, a NAS connects to your network, which involves a more complex setup. Once configured, it can be accessed by multiple devices, including Macs, iPhones, and iPads, either through the Finder, a dedicated app, or a web browser.
 This comprehensive approach helps us determine not just the raw speed of a NAS drive, but also its practicality and user-friendliness in a typical home or office environment. You can learn more about the pros and cons of using a NAS for storage or how they support features like Time Machine for backups.

 How many NAS bays do you need?
 Two bays
 Two bays are enough for documents, family photos, computer backups, and a modest media collection. RAID 1 provides a mirrored copy when one drive fails, but it also means roughly half the raw drive capacity is usable. Two bays leave little room for growth and can make a large migration more disruptive.
 Four bays
 Four bays are the best default for a serious home user. They allow RAID 5 or a comparable single-drive-fault-tolerant arrangement, provide more capacity efficiency than RAID 1, and make gradual expansion easier. Four bays also provide more headroom for photo indexing, media services, containers, and multiple users.
 Five or eight bays
 Consider five or eight bays for a large media library, video editing, multiple backup targets, several concurrent users, surveillance storage, or a home lab. They are excessive for ordinary family backups unless you expect rapid growth.
 RAID is not a backup
 RAID primarily improves availability after certain drive failures. It does not protect against theft, fire, ransomware, accidental deletion, a bad administrator, or a failed NAS enclosure.
 RAID 1: two drives mirror each other; usable capacity is approximately one drive.
 RAID 5: generally uses one drive’s worth of capacity for parity and tolerates one drive failure.
 RAID 6: uses more parity but can tolerate two drive failures.
 SHR and similar flexible systems: can simplify expansion with mixed drive sizes on supported platforms.
 RAID 0 or JBOD: should not be the only location for irreplaceable data.
 Actual usable capacity is lower than the arithmetic because of parity, filesystem overhead, reserved space, and vendor conventions. Four drives do not produce four drives’ worth of usable protected storage.
 A practical home backup plan
 Use a version of the 3-2-1 approach:
 Keep at least three copies of important data.
 Use two different storage systems or media.
 Keep one copy off-site.
 For example, the NAS can hold the primary family library, an external USB drive can hold a scheduled backup, and encrypted cloud storage or a remote NAS can provide the off-site copy. Use file versioning, snapshots, recycle bins, or replication where appropriate, but do not treat snapshots as a disconnected backup. An attacker with administrative control may be able to delete them.
 Test restoration. A completed backup job only proves that data was copied; it does not prove that you can recover the files you need.

 Plex and Jellyfin: direct play versus transcoding
 “Supports Plex” does not mean that every file will play smoothly. There are three different workloads:
 Direct play: the client supports the original video and audio formats, so the NAS does little work.
 Remuxing: the container changes while the video stream remains the same; this is generally lighter than transcoding.
 Transcoding: the NAS converts the video or audio into a format the client can play; this can be CPU- or GPU-intensive.
 Hardware transcoding matters most for remote streaming, incompatible televisions, subtitles, and 4K HDR-to-1080p conversion. Plex hardware transcoding may require Plex Pass, depending on the setup. Jellyfin has its own hardware-acceleration requirements.

 Hard drives, SSDs, and compatibility
 NAS-rated hard drives are designed for continuous operation and vibration environments, but “NAS-rated” does not automatically mean every drive is ideal for every workload. Check workload ratings, firmware, warranty terms, noise, and the manufacturer’s model-specific compatibility list.
 SSD-only NAS systems are quiet and fast but usually cost more per terabyte.  Mixed-size drives can be useful with flexible RAID systems, but usable capacity is often limited by the smallest drives in an array. Starting with one drive and adding another later may be possible, but migration depends on the platform and requires a separate backup during the process.
 Security checklist
 Change or disable the default administrator account.
 Use a unique, long password.
 Enable multifactor authentication.
 Install firmware and application updates promptly.
 Avoid exposing the NAS management interface directly to the public Internet.
 Prefer a VPN or carefully configured vendor relay service for remote access.
 Disable services you do not use.
 Give each person only the permissions they need.
 Keep an offline or otherwise isolated backup.
 Test that you can restore files.
 A vendor relay can simplify remote access, but it is not a guarantee of safety. Account security, permissions, updates, and configuration still matter. NASCompares’ 2026 software comparison also emphasizes strong passwords, updates, multifactor authentication, limited Internet exposure, snapshots, and separate backups.
 NAS versus cloud storage, USB drives, and a mini-PC
 A NAS is worthwhile when several devices need shared storage, a household has a large local library, or automatic backups and private-cloud access justify the administration. It may be a poor fit for one laptop, little local data, or someone who does not want to maintain a server.
 For a single computer, an external drive plus cloud backup is often simpler and cheaper. A NAS also does not eliminate electricity, drive replacement, remote-access maintenance, or off-site backup costs.
 A mini-PC with external storage can be better for Docker, virtual machines, Linux, or media transcoding. Its disadvantages are more setup, less integrated drive monitoring, and less polished backup software. A direct-attached storage enclosure is another good choice when only one computer needs access.
 Total cost of ownership
 Calculate the complete system rather than comparing empty enclosures:
 NAS enclosure.
 NAS-rated hard drives or SSDs.
 External USB backup drive.
 Cloud or remote-NAS backup.
 UPS with USB signaling if possible.
 2.5GbE or 10GbE switch and adapters.
 Optional NVMe drives, memory, or expansion unit.
 Replacement drives and electricity over time.
 Prices and availability change quickly. Treat retailer sale prices and dated reviews as temporary signals, and verify the current US price, diskless or populated configuration, warranty, and drive compatibility before buying.
 Situations to avoid
 Do not choose a two-bay NAS for a rapidly expanding library simply because it is cheaper today.
 Do not choose an ARM NAS for demanding transcoding without verifying the exact workload.
 Do not give a nontechnical family an immature software platform solely for stronger hardware.
 Do not treat RAID as the only protection for irreplaceable photos.
 Do not buy 10GbE without compatible clients, switches, and storage.
 Do not buy SSD cache before funding adequate capacity and a second backup.
 Do not select a surveillance NAS from a maximum camera-count claim alone; retention, resolution, codecs, motion detection, drives, and other workloads all affect the result.
 Final buying advice
 Choose the Synology DS425+ if you want the easiest balanced solution for household backups, photos, shared files, and four-bay growth. Choose the DS225+ if your needs are modest and mirrored two-drive storage is enough. Choose the UGREEN DXP4800 Pro or TerraMaster F4-424 Pro when Plex, Jellyfin, containers, and hardware value matter more than the most mature software ecosystem. Choose the QNAP TS-464 for flexible apps, expansion, and advanced networking. Choose the DS925+ when you want mainstream software plus a longer capacity runway. Choose TrueNAS, Unraid, or a mini-PC build only if you are comfortable administering the system yourself.

 The Synology DS1525+ is the best overall choice for most Mac households and small offices. It has five bays, dual 2.5GbE, SMB support, two M.2 NVMe slots, optional 10GbE, and expansion to as many as 15 drives. The QNAP TS-464 is a strong four-bay alternative.

 Choose a NAS that explicitly supports Time Machine over SMB. Apple does not recommend AFP-based NAS backups for newer macOS versions and says AFP will not be supported in macOS 27 or later.

 No. RAID can keep some data available after particular drive failures, but it does not protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or total NAS failure. Keep an independent off-site or offline backup.

 The Synology DS1525+ is sold without drives. You must add compatible internal SATA hard drives or SSDs, then create a storage pool and volume. Budget for the enclosure, drives, UPS, and independent backup together.
 How many NAS bays do I need for a Mac?
 A two-bay NAS can be enough for one Mac and a modest library. A four- or five-bay NAS is preferable for several Macs, large photo libraries, active video projects, or long-term expansion.

Past that non-negotiable, the differences come down to how well each NAS manages sparse bundle growth, multiple Macs on one box, and initial backup speed.
 Below are 8 NAS devices we evaluated on SMB3 readiness, per-Mac quota management, RAM for running Time Machine alongside other services, and true cost with drives included, ranging from a $199.99 diskless 2-bay for a single MacBook to a $619.99 five-core 4-bay built for a household running Time Machine on several Macs at once.
 5 Criteria to Look For Before Buying a NAS for Mac and Time Machine Backup
 Key buying criteria so you get the right fit the first time.
 Remember every listed NAS here is diskless, budget drives separately
 The price shown for a NAS enclosure covers the hardware chassis, CPU, and RAM only, not the actual storage drives, NAS-grade drives built for 24/7 operation like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red still need to be budgeted on top, often adding $80 to $200 or more per bay depending on capacity and drive type.
 This matters because comparing NAS units purely by enclosure price without factoring in drive cost gives a misleading picture of the real total investment, a cheaper enclosure with more bays to fill can end up costing more overall than a pricier enclosure with fewer bays.
 Check whether a listing is diskless or ships with drives included, and add realistic per-bay drive costs to the enclosure price before comparing total cost across options.
 Weigh CPU class and RAM over bay count for real day-to-day performance
 Bay count determines maximum storage capacity, but CPU architecture (Intel, AMD, or ARM) and RAM amount determine how well the NAS actually handles real workloads, running apps, transcoding media on the fly, or serving multiple simultaneous users, and a higher bay count with a weak CPU can bottleneck performance regardless of how much raw storage it holds.
 This matters more the more the NAS will do beyond simple file storage, like Plex transcoding or running multiple docker containers, less if it's purely a basic backup target.
 Check the specific CPU model and RAM amount (and whether RAM is upgradeable) rather than choosing primarily by bay count.
 Understand RAID as a rebuild-time safety net, not a substitute for real backup
 RAID configurations protect against a single drive failure by letting the array rebuild from redundant data, but RAID is not a backup, it does nothing to protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a controller failure that affects the whole array at once.
 This distinction matters because treating RAID redundancy as sufficient backup protection is a common and genuinely risky misunderstanding, a real backup strategy needs a copy of critical data stored somewhere physically separate from the NAS itself.
 Check what RAID level a given NAS supports, and separately plan an actual backup strategy, ideally following a 3-2-1 approach, rather than relying on RAID redundancy alone.
 Match drive type (HDD vs SSD/NVMe) to your actual access pattern
 Traditional hard drives offer the lowest cost per terabyte for bulk storage like media libraries or backups, while SSD or NVMe-based NAS storage costs significantly more per terabyte but delivers much faster random access speeds, genuinely useful for frequently-accessed files, active project work, or serving as a fast cache tier.
 This matters directly based on how you'll actually use the storage, a media library accessed sequentially benefits little from SSD speed, while an active working file share benefits considerably.
 Check whether the NAS supports the drive type you need, and weigh the real cost-per-terabyte difference against how much you'll actually benefit from faster random access.
 Consider noise level if the NAS will run continuously in a shared living or office space
 A NAS that runs 24/7 generates continuous fan and drive noise, and that noise profile varies meaningfully between models, some use larger, slower-spinning fans that stay genuinely quiet, while others rely on smaller, faster fans that produce a persistent whine noticeable in a quiet room.
 This matters a great deal if the NAS will sit in a bedroom, living room, or shared home office rather than a dedicated closet or basement out of earshot.
 Check reviews specifically for real-world noise level mentions during continuous operation, not just idle noise, since drive activity and fan speed both increase under load.

 When to Spend More
 Spend more if
 You need real multi-user performance, media transcoding, or business-critical reliability, where UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Plus's CPU and RAM give real headroom over the cheaper picks.
 Save if
 You just need simple backup storage for one or two users, where UGREEN NAS DH2300 covers the same job at a lower price.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Will my Time Machine backups stop working because AFP is being removed?
 If your NAS is still configured to use AFP, yes, backups will silently stop once your Mac updates past macOS 27. Every NAS in this list supports SMB3 with Bonjour/mDNS advertising, which is the protocol combination Apple is standardizing on, but confirm SMB3 is actually enabled in your sharing settings rather than assuming it by default.
 Why does my Time Machine backup keep growing and filling up the NAS?
 Time Machine stores backups in a sparse bundle disk image that expands automatically over time, and without a manually set quota it will keep growing until it consumes all available NAS space. Set a quota in the NAS admin panel during initial setup, a common recommendation is roughly 1.5x your Mac's internal storage capacity.
 Can multiple Macs back up to the same NAS with Time Machine?
 Yes, but each Mac needs its own separate shared folder with its own quota. Using a single shared folder for more than one Mac's Time Machine backup will corrupt the backup history for both machines, so set up a dedicated folder per Mac even within the same household.
 How long does the first Time Machine backup take over a NAS?
 For a 512GB Mac, an initial full Time Machine backup over Wi-Fi can take 8-24 hours depending on your router, and considerably less over a wired Ethernet connection. Run the first backup wired if at all possible; incremental backups afterward are small enough to run comfortably over Wi-Fi.
 How do I know my Time Machine backup will actually restore if I need it?
 A backup can appear to complete successfully for months while quietly failing to produce a restorable image due to RAID errors or file corruption. Periodically, at least once a quarter, test an actual file or folder restore from the backup rather than relying on Time Machine's success indicator alone.
 Do drive compatibility warnings mean I bought the wrong drive?
 Not necessarily. Some 2024-and-newer Plus-tier NAS models show a compatibility warning in the admin panel for any drive that isn't the manufacturer's own branded line, even when a reputable third-party NAS drive like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red works fine. It's worth knowing before you buy so the warning doesn't seem like a hardware failure.
 Bottom Line

So the drive died on a Tuesday. No click of death, no grinding, none of the dramatic stuff you read about on forums -- it just sat there being a warm brick while I moved it between USB ports like that was going to fix anything. Three years of photos. RIP.

That was the week I gave up and bought a NAS.

It has been on the shelf above my desk ever since, which is long enough to have opinions, and long enough to admit that most of the specs I agonised over beforehand did not matter much. The one I nearly skipped is the one that mattered most. Labor Day weekend tends to be when people finally deal with the drawer full of drives, so here is how I would choose now, plus the eight machines on Newegg I keep sending to friends who text me about this at 11pm.

What Actually Changed, Day to Day

On paper, a NAS is a small computer whose entire personality is holding drives and sharing them over your network. Thrilling stuff.

In practice my phone dumps photos onto it over Wi-Fi without me doing anything, my laptop and my desktop see the same folders, and when a drive eventually dies -- one will, they all do -- the array keeps running while I swap it out. There is also a physical thing nobody mentions in reviews, which is that you can hear it. Not loud, just a faint seek-chatter from the shelf when I drag a big folder across, and I have come to find that oddly reassuring. Like the box is nodding at me.

What I will not oversell: this is not a backup. Redundancy saves you from a dead drive. It does not save you from deleting the wrong folder at 1am, or from ransomware, or from the radiator upstairs deciding to have a moment. I still keep a copy somewhere else. The NAS is where everything lives, not where everything is safe.

The Four Specs I Check, In That Order

Bays. Two is the floor if you want redundancy, because a mirrored pair survives one dead drive. Two is also the number most people quietly regret about eight months later. Four or more opens up RAID 5 or 6 and uses your capacity more efficiently. Buy one bay more than you think you need -- I have never once met someone who regretted the spare slot.

Network speed. This is the one I nearly ignored and it turned out to decide how the whole thing feels. Plain gigabit caps you around 110MB/s no matter how quick the drives are, which is fine right up until the first time you move a folder of video and end up making tea. Almost everything worth buying in 2026 has at least 2.5GbE.

Processor. ARM is fine for files and backups. Want to transcode video, run Docker containers or host a VM? Get x86 and stop thinking about it.

Memory. Matters the moment you start running apps, and whether you can add more varies wildly. Some models solder it down. Check the listing, not the brand.

The Field at a Glance
Model	Bays	Processor	Networking	Best for
Synology BeeStation Plus	1 (8TB included)	Not published	Wired Ethernet	Zero-setup personal cloud
Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2	2	Realtek RTD1619B	2.5GbE	Cheapest real NAS
Synology DS225+	2	Intel Celeron J4125	2.5GbE + 1GbE	The safe first NAS
UGREEN NASync DH4300 Plus	4	Rockchip 8-core ARM	2.5GbE	Most bays, least fuss
TERRAMASTER F4-425 Plus	4 + 3x M.2	Intel N95	Dual 5GbE	Fastest networking here
Synology DS1525+	5 + 2x M.2	AMD Ryzen R1600	Dual 2.5GbE	Room to grow
ASUSTOR FLASHSTOR 6	6x M.2 NVMe	Intel Celeron N5105	Dual 2.5GbE	Silent, all-flash
Seagate IronWolf 8TB	Drive	--	SATA 6Gb/s	Filling any of the above
If You Just Want It To Work: Synology BeeStation Plus
Drives included, RAID decisions skipped. The NAS for people who do not want a NAS.

Some people do not want to learn what RAID is. Completely reasonable position, honestly.

The Synology BeeStation Plus 8TB ships with its 8TB drive already inside and 4GB of DDR4, so there is nothing to assemble and nothing to configure past signing in. I set one up for my parents over a weekend visit and the whole thing took less time than the coffee did -- two cables, one login, done. It handles up to eight separate user accounts with their own storage, pulls photos in automatically from phones and from iCloud, and works with Plex. It is a single-drive device, so what you get is ownership rather than redundancy. Pair it with a copy somewhere else.

The Cheapest Way In: Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2

The Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 AS1202T is where I would start rather than a cheaper single-bay box, because two bays means a mirror. Quad-core Realtek RTD1619B at 1.7GHz, 1GB of DDR4, and -- crucially -- a 2.5GbE port instead of plain gigabit. The drives slide in without screws, which sounds like a small thing until you have done it the other way with a tiny screwdriver and a bad desk lamp. That 1GB of memory is the ceiling on ambition though. File server and backup target, not an app platform.

The One I Suggest Most Often: Synology DS225+

Ask me for one recommendation with no other information and I say the Synology DS225+. Intel Celeron J4125, 2GB of DDR4 across two SODIMM slots and expandable to 6GB, one 2.5GbE port plus a 1GbE port. The hardware is competent rather than exciting. What you are actually buying is Synology's software, which is the most forgiving place on earth to learn what any of this means at 11pm on a Sunday.

Most Bays for the Least Fuss: UGREEN NASync DH4300 Plus

The UGREEN NASync DH4300 Plus gets you four bays and 8GB of LPDDR4X on an eight-core Rockchip ARM processor, with a 2.5GbE port and RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, 10, JBOD and Basic. Maximum raw capacity is 128TB. One thing to know going in: that 8GB is soldered. What ships is what you get, forever.

Fastest Networking Here: TERRAMASTER F4-425 Plus
Two 5GbE ports and three M.2 slots -- the one to buy if you move video.

This is the box I would buy if my job involved large files. The TERRAMASTER F4-425 Plus runs a quad-core Intel N95 with 8GB of memory, four SATA bays and three M.2 NVMe slots, behind two 5GbE ports with link aggregation -- TerraMaster quotes up to 1020MB/s sequential. It also does 4K and 8K hardware transcoding, runs Docker and virtual machines, and plays nicely with Plex, Emby and Jellyfin. Maximum raw capacity is listed at 144TB. The aluminium shell is also genuinely cold to the touch, which after a summer of listening to a plastic box breathe is a small luxury.

Room to Grow: Synology DS1525+

Five bays is where a NAS stops being a photo dump and starts being infrastructure. The Synology DS1525+ uses an AMD Ryzen R1600 with 8GB of ECC memory expandable to 16GB, five drive bays plus two M.2 2280 NVMe slots for cache, and two 2.5GbE ports with a 10GbE upgrade path. It also expands to fifteen drives with two DX525 units, which is really the point. You are buying headroom, not capacity.

Silent and All-Flash: ASUSTOR FLASHSTOR 6

No spinning drives, no noise. Thats the whole argument for the ASUSTOR FLASHSTOR 6 (FS6706T), and if the box lives in the room where you sleep it is the only argument that matters. Six M.2 NVMe slots, a quad-core Intel Celeron N5105, 4GB of DDR4-2933 expandable to 16GB, dual 2.5GbE and an HDMI 2.0b output, pulling around 18W in normal use. I have stood next to one while it copied a hundred gigabytes and heard nothing at all, which was mildly unsettling.

Do Not Cheap Out on the Drives
NAS-rated drives put up with their neighbours shaking. Desktop drives were not asked to.

Every diskless box above needs drives and this is not the place to save. The Seagate IronWolf 8TB is a 7200 RPM CMR drive with 256MB of cache on SATA 6Gb/s, rated for a 180TB annual workload and 1 million hours MTBF, with rotational vibration sensors so drives in a multi-bay chassis do not disturb each other.

That last bit is the actual reason NAS drives exist, and it stops being abstract the first time you hold four of them. They have real heft, like hardcover books, and four of them spinning up together makes the whole enclosure hum for about two seconds before it settles.

How I Would Choose

Buy the BeeStation Plus if you want the problem gone tonight. Buy the DS225+ if you want to learn this properly and then never think about it again. Go F4-425 Plus if you edit video, DS1525+ if the collection is clearly going to keep growing, FLASHSTOR 6 if the box has to be silent.

Whatever you pick: NAS-rated drives, and buy the capacity now rather than later. Browse the current lineup in Newegg's network attached storage listings.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many bays do I actually need? Two is the minimum if you want to survive a drive failure, because a mirrored pair keeps running when one drive dies. Four or more lets you use RAID 5 or 6, which gives you more usable capacity from the same number of drives. My rule is to buy one bay more than your current plan, since adding bays later usually means buying a whole new enclosure.

Is 2.5GbE worth it over plain gigabit? Yes, and it is the upgrade people notice most. Gigabit tops out around 110MB/s, which a single modern hard drive can saturate on its own. Every multi-bay model in this guide has at least 2.5GbE, and the TERRAMASTER F4-425 Plus goes to two 5GbE ports. You will need a switch and a network adapter that match to see the benefit.

Do I need special NAS hard drives? For a multi-bay enclosure running around the clock, yes. NAS drives like the IronWolf carry higher annual workload ratings and include rotational vibration sensors, because drives mounted next to each other physically shake one another. Desktop drives are built on the assumption they are alone in a quiet case.

Does RAID mean I do not need backups? No, and this is the most expensive misunderstanding in home storage. RAID protects against hardware failure only. It will happily replicate a deleted file, a corrupted file or an encrypted-by-ransomware file across every drive. Keep at least one copy somewhere the NAS cannot reach.

Best NAS for Small Business Backup and File Storage (2026 Buyer's Guide) - IP Security Depot 
 Skip to main content 
 In this article 
 Quick Answer 
 The right small-business NAS is decided by bay count, network speed and where the box lives, not by brand. Pick enough bays to survive a parity rebuild, enough network to finish the backup window, and a chassis that fits the room you actually have.
 Best rack NAS for multi-user backup: Ubiquiti UNAS-PRO — seven 2.5/3.5-inch bays, 10G SFP+ uplink, 2U chassis.
 Best quiet desktop NAS for an office: QNAP HS-264-8G-US — fanless 2-bay, Intel Celeron N5105, dual 2.5GbE.
 Best all-flash NAS for shared project files: QNAP TBS-464-8G-US — four M.2 NVMe slots, dual 2.5GbE bondable to 5 Gbps.
 Best compact NAS for branch and UniFi sites: Ubiquiti UNAS-2-B — 2 bays, 2.5 GbE, runs entirely on PoE++.
 Best offsite rotation target: QNAP TR-002-US — 2-bay hardware-RAID enclosure over USB 3.2 Gen 2 at 10Gbps.
 Best capacity expansion when the NAS is full: QNAP TL-D1600S-US — sixteen SATA bays in a desktop JBOD shelf.
 This guide is for the person who owns IT at a company with ten to a hundred seats: the office manager who inherited a file share, the integrator adding a backup target next to a recorder, the MSP standardizing branch storage. It covers the network storage we stock and ship today, the capacity and bandwidth math that decides which one fits, and the difference between a snapshot and a backup — a distinction that costs people their data every year. If your storage job is video retention rather than files, start with how to size NVR hard drives without guessing , then come back here. Everything below is in the network attached storage category.
 Start With the Workload, Not the Bay Count
 Bay count is the first number everyone asks about and the last one that should drive the decision. Three very different jobs get called "NAS," and they stress the hardware in opposite directions.
 A backup target. Write-heavy, almost entirely sequential, read only during a restore or a test. It needs capacity and parity far more than it needs CPU. The failure mode that matters is a second drive dying during a rebuild, so bay count is really a redundancy decision, not a capacity one.
 An active file share. Twenty people opening, saving and searching documents all day is random I/O with bursty concurrency. Here the processor, the memory ceiling and the network interface decide whether the share feels instant or feels like 2009. Spinning disks handle it; flash handles it better.
 A continuous ingest archive. Camera streams and log pipelines write around the clock and never stop to let a rebuild finish. Sustained write throughput and drive class matter more than peak numbers, and the box needs to be sized so that a degraded array still keeps up.
 Why it matters. A fanless two-bay unit is an excellent file share for a quiet office and a poor primary backup target for a company with real retention requirements. A seven-bay rack unit is the opposite. Buying one chassis to do all three jobs is how small businesses end up with a single point of failure holding both the live data and its only copy.
 How We Picked
 We limited the field to network and direct-attached storage sitting in our warehouse today, then shortlisted on the criteria that change an install outcome rather than a spec sheet:
 Enough bays for the parity scheme you actually need. Two bays means RAID 1 and a 50% capacity tax. Four or more opens RAID 5; six or more makes RAID 6 sensible, which is the first configuration that survives a second failure during a rebuild. Bay count sets your risk floor.
 A network port faster than gigabit. Gigabit Ethernet tops out around 110 MB/s in practice, and that single number has stretched more backup windows past sunrise than any drive. Every pick here runs 2.5GbE or faster, because the uplink is usually the bottleneck long before the disks are.
 A form factor that fits the room. Rack units need depth, airflow and a cabinet. Desktop units need a surface, quiet operation and a nearby outlet. One pick here needs no outlet at all. Placement kills more deployments than performance does.
 An honest growth path. Storage demand only moves one direction. We favored units that can take mixed-capacity drives, bond links, or attach an expansion shelf, so phase two is not a forklift replacement.
 Ubiquiti UNAS-PRO — Best Rack NAS for Multi-User Backup and File Storage
 Drive bays: 7, 2.5-inch or 3.5-inch, mixed capacities supported · Network: (1) 10G SFP+, 10G/1G · RAID: 5 or 6 parity schemes · OS: UniFi OS · Power: AC/DC input, 160W · Dimensions: 442.4 × 325 × 87.4 mm · Form: 2U rack-mount, standard 19-inch
 Seven bays is the number that makes this unit worth racking. It is the point where RAID 6 stops feeling expensive — you give up two drives to parity and still keep five working for you, which means a drive can fail, and a second can fail mid-rebuild, without the array going with it. The 10G SFP+ uplink removes the gigabit ceiling that defines most small-business backup windows, turning a multi-hour nightly job into something that finishes before anyone notices. Two honest trade-offs. First, that is one network port, not two, so there is no link redundancy and you need an available SFP+ port or transceiver on the switch; plan the uplink before the unit arrives. Second, UniFi OS is a different philosophy from the app-store-driven NAS operating systems — provisioning and access control flow from the UniFi console you may already run, which is clean if you live in that ecosystem and limiting if your plan depends on third-party packages. Verify that before you commit.
 Shop the Ubiquiti UNAS-PRO → 
 QNAP HS-264-8G-US — Best Fanless NAS for a Quiet Office
 Drive bays: 2, 3.5-inch SATA 6Gb/s · CPU: Intel Celeron N5105, 4-core / 4-thread, 2.0 GHz base, 2.9 GHz burst, 10W TDP · Memory: 8GB DDR4, non-expandable · Network: dual 2.5GbE · Cooling: fanless, passive heatsink chassis · Form: compact desktop
 Not every storage decision happens in a server room. When the NAS has to live in a conference room, a reception closet or an AV rack ten feet from someone's desk, acoustic output is the spec that makes or breaks the placement, and this chassis has none — no fan, nothing to fail mechanically on the cooling side. The N5105's four cores handle indexing, a backup job and media transcoding at the same time without the stalls older dual-core units hit, and dual 2.5GbE means the share is not throttled to gigabit the moment two people copy large files. The trade-offs are structural, not flaws. Passive cooling means thermal headroom is the hard constraint, so it wants free air around it and not a stack of gear on top. The 8GB of memory is soldered, so a roadmap with multiple virtual machines on it should look elsewhere now rather than discover the ceiling later. And two bays means RAID 1, which is mirroring, not capacity.
 Shop the QNAP HS-264-8G-US → 
 QNAP TBS-464-8G-US — Best All-Flash NAS for Shared Project Files
 Drive bays: 4 × M.2 2280 NVMe Gen3 x2, no SATA bottleneck · CPU: Intel Celeron N5105, 4-core / 4-thread, burst to 2.9 GHz, AES-NI · Memory: 8 GB DDR4, fixed · Network: dual 2.5GbE, bondable to 5 Gbps aggregate · Video: dual HDMI outputs · Form: all-flash desktop NASbook, no spinning drives
 This is the pick for teams whose complaint is latency, not capacity: design files, shared databases, virtual machine images, or any workload where a dozen people hammer the same folder and spinning disks spend their day seeking. Four NVMe slots on PCIe Gen3 x2 mean the drives are not the limit — bond both 2.5GbE ports to a capable switch for up to 5 Gbps and the network is still the ceiling, which is the right problem to have. AES-NI in the processor means volume encryption costs almost nothing in CPU, so encrypting a share holding client data is a decision you can make on the merits. The trade-off is cost per terabyte and the capacity ceiling that comes with it; flash is not where bulk archive belongs. Memory is fixed at 8 GB, so treat container and VM plans as a hard budget. The practical pattern is flash here for live work, parity disk elsewhere for retention.
 Shop the QNAP TBS-464-8G-US → 
 Ubiquiti UNAS-2-B — Best Compact NAS for Branch and UniFi Sites
 Drive bays: 2 × 3.5-inch, up to 16TB each · Network: 1 × 2.5 GbE, 1 × USB-C · Power: PoE++ (802.3bt), adapter included, no separate outlet required · Weight: 2.85 lbs · Capacity: 4–8 concurrent camera streams, 7–30 day rolling retention depending on resolution and frame rate · Management: UniFi Network console · Form: compact desktop or rack
 Multi-site organizations keep running into the same wall: each branch needs local storage, but nobody wants a separate NAS login and licensing scheme per location. This unit answers that narrowly and well. Storage policies, disk health alerts and retention schedules live in the same UniFi console as the cameras and switches, which means one dashboard for a dozen sites instead of a dozen logins. Running entirely on PoE++ from the included adapter is the underrated part: in a wall-mounted closet with one data drop and no spare receptacle, that is the difference between installing today and scheduling an electrician. At 2.85 lbs it mounts almost anywhere, and the USB-C port covers direct-attach backup or emergency recovery. Be clear-eyed about scope. It is purpose-built for on-premise recording and archival in a UniFi deployment, two bays means mirroring, and the stated stream and retention figures are the honest working envelope — not a general-purpose file server for a headquarters.
 Shop the Ubiquiti UNAS-2-B → 
 QNAP TR-002-US — Best Offsite Rotation Target
 Drive bays: 2 × 3.5-inch SATA · Interface: USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, 10Gbps · RAID: hardware RAID 0, 1, JBOD and individual, set by onboard selector, no drivers · Weight: 3.02 lbs net, 3.4 lbs gross · Operating temperature: 0–40 °C · Form: desktop direct-attached enclosure
 The third copy in a 3-2-1 plan has to leave the building, and for a small business that usually means a drive set that someone carries home or to a safe deposit box. This enclosure is the cleanest version of that: two 3.5-inch drives, hardware RAID handled by the enclosure's own microprocessor rather than the host, and a 10Gbps Type-C link so the weekly copy does not take a shift. Because parity runs on board, there is no driver stack to maintain and no host dependency on the array format. It also serves as plain capacity expansion for a NAS or workstation that has run out of internal bays. Three things to plan for. It is direct-attached, not networked, so it needs a host and is not a backup destination for the whole office on its own. Full 10Gbps requires a genuine USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C path — a Type-A adapter drops to the host port's speed. And 2.5-inch drives need a bracket that is not included.
 Shop the QNAP TR-002-US → 
 QNAP TL-D1600S-US — Best Capacity Expansion When the NAS Is Full
 Drive bays: 16 · Drive interface: SATA, HDD or SSD · Form: desktop chassis · Drives: sold separately · Role: JBOD expansion for a compatible host NAS
 Every growing company eventually fills a NAS and faces the same choice: replace the platform, or add bays. Sixteen SATA slots in one shelf is the add-bays answer at a scale that actually buys several years — the right shape for footage archives, bulk file retention and backup targets where drive count matters more than peak speed. Because it is a JBOD shelf rather than a standalone appliance, it keeps your existing volumes, users and shares intact; growth becomes incremental instead of a weekend migration. The non-negotiable prerequisite: your host NAS must support SATA JBOD expansion and must list this unit, so confirm the model against QNAP's compatibility list before ordering, not after. It is also a desktop chassis, which means shelf or table space rather than rack units — convenient in a branch with no cabinet, awkward in a tidy server room. Populating sixteen bays is a meaningful power and heat addition to whatever room it lands in, so check the circuit and the airflow first.
